an3.65:1.1: This is a key text in understanding Buddhist modernism, often cited by 20th century teachers as a Buddhist “charter of free inquiry”. Its content is not unusual for the Pali suttas (see eg. ([mn95](), [mn101](), [mn102](), [sn12.68](), [sn35.153](), [an3.66](), [an4.193]())), but the context has a modern ring: how to present the teachings to a skeptical audience, weary of different teachings. | The discourse is usually named Kālāmasutta today, but the colophons typically name it _kesaputtiyā_, “the Kesiyans”. The variant _kesamuttiyā_ would mean “those of loosed hair” and seems unlikely. The title in the MS edition, _kesamuttisutta_, appears to be an unwarranted abridgment of the already-implausible variant.
an3.65:1.2: The Kālāmas are barely attested in ancient literature, being remembered only here and as the clan of Āḷāra ([mn26:15.1]()) and Bharaṇḍu ([an3.126:3.3]()). Their name is uncertain; perhaps Sanskrit _kālāpa_ in the sense “members of the group”; the p/m substitution is also felt in _kesaputta_. | The town of Kesaputta is likewise poorly attested. It perhaps modern Kesariya, where there is a large ancient Buddhist monument. The brāhmaṇas mention a certain Dālbhya of the Keśiyans, who struggled to complete the rites of kingship (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.8.4), and to find a priest to intone the verses correctly (Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa 13.10.8; Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa 3.29.1–3.31.1); these are perhaps coded stories of the difficulties in establishing Vedic rites as the Aryan culture spread east. Dālbhya was said to be a founding king of the Pañcāla realm (Kāṭhaka Saṁhitā 30.2; see J.P. Sharma. *Republics in Ancient India*, pp. 231–6), his people one of the three (or five) clans that made up that nation. It is possible that Kesaputta and its people the Kesiyans are descended from a branch of the same people, having settled even further east. Pali commentaries say they had a democratic republican governance, which may well have been so, but from their appearance here it is clear they are under Kosalan sovereignty and can hardly claim the status of an independent republic. Likely the town was nestled between the river Sarayū and the Mallakas to the north, the Ganges to the south, and Varanasi to the southwest.
an3.65:3.8: Not all doubt is a hindrance; it’s necessary in cases that demand it. | The items below are a stock set of grounds for belief, which play a limited role in supporting the search for truth, but do not yield definitive answers. The list can be grouped in synonyms. Textual authority is emphasized in the items from oral tradition to canonical authority ([mn76:24.1]()), which were asserted by some brahmins to be reliable sources of truth ([mn95:12.11]()). From logic to acceptance of a view ([mn76:27.1]()) are charactersitic of those ascetics who relied on logical inquiry, and the final two.
an3.65:4.1: “Oral transmission” (_anussava_), literally “after-hearing”; in the culture of the time it meant not passed down by hearing from another in the oral tradition. Most famous from the Buddha’s first sermon, where he declared his teaching was “not learned before from another” ([sn56.11:5.1](); see note on [mn95:14.1]()). | “Lineage” (_paramparā_), literally “from next to next”, is a concept the Buddha would have been familiar with from his days with Brahmanical teachers, who compiled lists of teachers (_vaṁśa_) stemming back to Brahmā (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.6.1, Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka 15.1). While the Buddha was at pains to distance himself from this practice, it was incorporated into late canonical texts ([pli-tv-pvr1.1:61.55]()), and memorizing such lists became an essential of monastic life ([pli-tv-pvr7:64.22]()). | “Testament” (_itikirā_), literally “so it seems”, is similar or identical to  _itihitiha_ (“so indeed, so indeed”, [snp5.9:1.5]()) and _itihāsa_ (“so it was”, [an3.59:1.4]()); the Buddhist version _itivuttaka_ (“so it was said”, [an4.6:1.9]()) is more epistemically cautious.  _Parivitakka_ means “train of thought”, as when the Buddha reads Kāpaṭika’s thoughts ([mn95:12.6]()). _Ākāra_ in this context means “reason”, as at [mn47:10.2](). | _Khanti_ is usually better rendered “acceptance” than the common “patience”.
